# Glenmore: the sale, what I have handled badly, and what is being kept

I want to put the whole of this in one place, rather than have it continue to travel around the family in pieces.

I have agreed the sale of the house at Glenmore, the old Mulkerrin place near Oughterard where Tom grew up. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**. I am putting that date here clearly because I do not want anybody hearing it second-hand, or wondering whether there is some part of the story I have left out.

Some of you heard about the sale before I had told you properly. That was my fault. I know Declan is very upset with me, and I know he is not the only one who may be hurt or taken aback. I am sorry for the way you found out. You should have heard it from me, directly and with enough explanation to make sense of it, not in a message or a chance remark from somebody else.

I am not sorry for making the decision to sell. I believe it is the decision I have to make. But those are two separate things, and I do not want to hide the first behind the second. I have handled parts of this badly, particularly with Declan. I hope this post will explain the decision honestly, including the parts I have not told you before, without pretending that I have been wise or calm about all of it.

I am not expecting everyone to read this and immediately agree with me. I would only ask you to read it before deciding what my reasons were.

## The sale, and the people who are buying

The house was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. I am very conscious that it is not just a house that happened to come into my possession. It is a Mulkerrin house, with a history long before me, and Tom’s childhood is in it. Other people in the family have their own memories and their own sense of what it represents. My being the person responsible for it now does not make all of that mine to dismiss.

The buyers are a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross. They have two small children, and they want to live in the house as their family home. They are not buying it to run as a holiday let.

The price they offered is fair. It is not the highest offer I received. There was a higher offer in the summer from buyers in Dublin, and I chose not to take it. I accepted the lower offer deliberately, because of who Aoife and Kevin are and what they intend to do with Glenmore.

I do not mention that to make myself sound generous, or to suggest that taking the lower offer settles every other question. It does not. People can still reasonably wish the house were staying in the family. But I want the facts to be plain: I did not simply take the largest amount of money put in front of me, and I was not indifferent to what would happen to the place after me.

What mattered to me was the thought of the house being lived in fully again. Not visited occasionally, not kept immaculate and empty, and not opened up for a few weeks of the year while remaining silent for the rest. There will be children there. There will be ordinary noise, school bags, meals, wet clothes and people coming in and out. Aoife and Kevin are buying a home, with all the work and responsibility that involves, not acquiring a sentimental idea of an old house in the country.

That does not make the sale painless. It does make it different, for me, from selling to somebody whose plans I could not feel any connection with.

## What Glenmore means to me

It would be very easy to write about roof surveys and maintenance costs and leave out the reasons this has been so difficult. I do not want to do that.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle were watching us. There was nothing grand about the setting, and nothing grand about either of us at that moment. It was just Tom, and me, and the rain, and those cattle standing there as if they had been invited as witnesses. It is one of the clearest memories of my life.

Our own children learned to swim in the lake below the house. I can still see Declan refusing to come out of the water until his lips were blue. No amount of telling him that he must be cold made the slightest difference. He was not cold, according to Declan, and even if he was, he was not coming out.

Those memories are not incidental to this decision. They are the reason it has taken me so long to reach it. I know what the back door, the haggard, the lake and the rooms inside that house hold for me. I also know that other people’s memories will not be exactly the same as mine, and that a place can be loved differently by different people without anybody being wrong.

For Declan, I understand that Glenmore is bound up with his father. When he said I was selling Dad, I did not want to hear it, but I understand the feeling underneath it now better than I did during that telephone call. When Tom is gone, and the house where he grew up is still standing, it can seem like one solid thing that remains. Letting it go can feel like permitting another loss.

I have had that feeling myself. I have stood in the house and thought that if I just kept it aired, kept the rain out and kept everything where it was, I would somehow be keeping faith with Tom. I did not want to be the person who disposed of the Mulkerrin place. Nor did I want to admit that the responsibility might be too much for me. It was easier to keep driving out and tell myself that I was managing.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I am not going to use that sentence as though he had foreseen these exact circumstances and given me instructions. He did not make this decision for me, and it would be too convenient now to put my decision into his mouth. But I knew Tom, and I knew what he meant when he said it. He did not love Glenmore because it was old, or because it preserved a version of the family fixed in one time. He loved it as a living place.

Over the best part of two years, I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. That realisation did not arrive suddenly, and it did not feel like relief at first. It felt almost like a betrayal. Now I think it is simply true. Tom is in what I remember, in what the children remember, in the stories that are told and retold, and in the lives that came after that wet day in the haggard. The house matters enormously, but it is not the only vessel for any of that.

## Why I cannot keep maintaining it

Tom died in March 2024. Since then, I have been driving out to Glenmore every fortnight. It is forty minutes each way. I open the place up and air it, check the pipes, and see what has changed since the previous visit.

Written down, a forty-minute drive every second week may not sound like very much. People will reasonably think that there are heavier burdens than that. Sometimes the journey itself was not the worst part. But the responsibility does not begin when I get into the car or end when I lock the door. An empty house does not stop needing things because nobody is living in it, and a fortnightly visit does not stop a roof or a chimney or a tank from deteriorating.

Ó Flaithearta’s carried out a roof survey in September. The slates and the back chimney need work, and the quote was **€38,000**. There is also damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing and would have to be dealt with in order to sell the house to anyone in any case.

I am not saying that one quotation, on its own, made the decision for me. Nor am I going to pretend there was a single morning when everything became simple. It is the accumulation of it: the work already needed, the work that would follow, the organising and overseeing of it, and the knowledge that there would still be an empty house at the end of it unless somebody came to live there. I cannot go on maintaining it, and I do not want to keep pretending that another year of fortnightly visits will somehow change that reality.

There is something else I have not told you.

Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I fell, and I lay there for about twenty minutes before I could get up. I told nobody until now. I am sorry that you are learning this in the middle of a blog post about a sale. I kept it to myself because I did not want the fuss, and because telling it would have meant admitting how much it had frightened me. Once it was said aloud, I would have had to answer questions I was not ready to answer.

Since then, I have been afraid of being alone at the house. Not every second, and not in some dramatic way that makes it impossible for me to cross the yard. But the fear is there. I am seventy-one. I am much more aware than I used to be of an empty house, a frosty step, a phone out of reach, and the length of time that might pass before anybody knew something was wrong.

I am not telling you about the fall to win an argument. It is not a trump card, and it does not mean everybody else must now say I was right. It happened, and it changed how I feel about going out there on my own. Leaving it out would give you a false account of why I reached this decision. I also should not have left people who care about me in the dark about it. That is another thing I handled by keeping quiet when silence was not necessarily the best choice.

The house did not become less precious to me because I became more frightened in it. That is what makes this so hard. If I had simply stopped loving Glenmore, selling it would be much easier to explain.

I know there may be a wish that everything could wait until Declan’s visit in the summer, so that we could all stand in the house together and discuss it then. I understand that wish, but I am not willing to postpone the decision until then. I cannot keep the responsibility suspended for months while I wait for a conversation that may still end with us disagreeing. The sale is agreed, and I intend to proceed with it. I know that will hurt Declan, and I am not going to dress that up as anything else.

## Declan

Declan heard about the sale from his cousin Gráinne on WhatsApp. He did not hear it from me.

He rang me at two in the morning, his time. He said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back to him that I should not have said. I am not going to repeat them here, because repeating them would do no good, and because I do not want to turn this post into a defence of myself by explaining how provoked I felt.

I was hurt and angry, and I let that come out in words I regret. He was ringing in shock and distress, and I answered him in a way that gave him more hurt. Whatever was said on either side, my part was mine, and I am sorry for it.

More importantly, I should have consulted Declan before agreeing the sale. Consulting him properly would not have guaranteed agreement. I might still have made the same decision, and he might still have opposed it. But he deserved the chance to hear my reasons before it was done, to say what the house meant to him, and to be angry with me in a conversation where at least he had all the facts. Instead, it arrived through a WhatsApp message, and then he had to absorb not only the sale but the feeling of having been left outside it.

That was wrong of me.

Declan, I know you read these posts, so I want to say this directly rather than hope it gets back to you. I am not angry with you. I am sorry for the way you found out, and I am sorry for my part in that telephone call. You do not have to agree with the sale for me to understand your upset. You do not have to tell me it is all right when it does not feel all right to you.

My door is open to you, and so is the conversation. You can ring me, write to me, or come and talk to me face to face. I am not asking you to pretend to be pleased, and I am not going to demand that we immediately make everything tidy between us. I only want you to know that there is no anger waiting for you here. I love you, and I regret that I did not bring you into this properly.

I also know that saying the door is open does not undo the fact that the decision has been made. I owe you honesty about both. The sale is proceeding, and I still want things to be right between us.

## What is staying in the family

I want everyone to know what is being kept. The house is being sold, but I am not walking away from its contents or its history.

The dresser is going to Úna’s. Pádraig’s fiddle is being kept. The photographs are being kept, as are the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. These things will remain with the family. The fiddle in particular is not merely an object that happened to be in a press. It carries Pádraig’s name and Tom’s connection to him, and it matters to me that it is not dispersed or forgotten.

The photographs will need time and care. I do not want them reduced to a few images that happen to suit one person’s version of the family. The house being cleared does not mean its whole story is being cleared away with it.

Aoife and Kevin have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. I am grateful to them for that. It is a kindness, and I want to acknowledge it without turning it into something it is not. After the sale closes, the house will be their home. We will not be entitled to wander into it or treat it as though nothing has changed. But their invitation means that the connection to the place need not be cut off completely at the gate on 15 January. We will still be able to go out, walk the land and remember, while respecting that a new family is living its own life there.

That is one of the things I am trying to hold on to: the difference between keeping a memory and keeping possession of every stone associated with it.

## Sunday 13 December

Before the house is cleared, I would like to have a family day out at Glenmore on **Sunday 13 December**.

Anyone who can come is welcome. We will have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because I would like people to be able to walk around properly and not spend the day worrying about their shoes. Come and see the house, walk down towards the lake, look at what is being kept, and tell whatever stories come to mind.

It does not have to be a day of brave faces. If you are sad, you can be sad. If you are angry with me, I would still rather see you than have you stay away for my comfort. I am not arranging the day as a celebration, because that word would not be honest for everybody. Nor do I want it to be a grim ceremony where nobody knows what to say. I would simply like us to have some time there together before the clearing begins.

To those of you in Boston, Perth and Leeds, I know that a Sunday at Glenmore is not a small undertaking. This is an invitation, not a test of anybody’s love for the family. There will be no roll call and no black marks for those who cannot make it. Work, flights, children, cost and the time of year are all real things. If you cannot be there, you are still very much part of this, and you are included in everything I have written here.

If you can come, please do. I would be glad of the company. I would like the children to be able to run about where they learned to swim, and for the people who have their own Glenmore stories to tell them aloud. Some of those stories may be ones I have forgotten, or ones I never knew. I would rather hear them in the house than have them disappear with the keys.

The sale closes on **15 January 2027**. There it is again, so nobody has to rely on a rumour or ask somebody else whether they have the date right. Between now and then there is the December day, the clearing to be done, and time for questions. If something here is unclear, ask me and I will answer as best I can. If you disagree with me, you can tell me that too.

I cannot promise that everyone will feel better about this after reading one long post. I only wanted to stop hiding behind silence and practicalities. I have sold the house because I cannot go on maintaining it, because I am afraid of being alone there since the fall, and because I have slowly become able to separate Tom’s memory from the continuing ownership of Glenmore. I chose buyers who will bring children and everyday life back into it, and I chose them knowingly, at a lower price than I was offered elsewhere.

None of that means the house was not loved. It was loved, and it is loved. That is why this hurts. But loving it does not require me to turn it into the museum Tom never wanted it to be, and remembering him does not require me to keep putting the key into that door when I no longer can.
